name: PT Wilmar Cahaya Indonesia Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Wilmar Cahaya: the spread, not the palm price, at a float discount
frontmatter.summary: CEKA refines and trades palm and wheat products on a thin spread and sells almost everything in Indonesia. The shares trade below book and below the cash the business generates, because a very small free float and a controlled register keep buyers away. We rate BUY: the spread has recovered, the group-pricing risk is now in the bear case, and the discount is structural, not an earnings verdict.
thesis: CEKA is a downstream palm refiner, not a planter. It buys essentially all of its feedstock and earns a refining and trading spread; the palm price moves revenue, not profit.
Gross margin recovered in 2026 after the FY2025 trough, and the palm-kernel line is growing faster than CPO, which is mix accretive.
The balance sheet carries no borrowings and the dividend has been paid every year since listing; the payout is the only reliable cash return in a small register.
The shares trade at a low multiple of depressed earnings and a discount to book, with a forward dividend yield that is high for an Indonesian staple.
The discount is a free-float and liquidity discount, which we apply explicitly; a controlled company with a small float can stay cheap, so the catalyst is cash return, not a re-rating.

catalysts.event: FY2026 full-year results and the declared dividend for the year
Annual general meeting approving the FY2026 dividend
Ramp-up of the Pontianak palm-kernel plant, whose work packages were targeted for completion between March and June 2026
CPO export duty and levy reset for the first quarter, which sets the domestic price environment

blocks.text: We initiate on PT Wilmar Cahaya Indonesia with a BUY and a target of Rp3,021 against Rp2,150, a total return of 48.8% including the Rp178 dividend we expect over the next twelve months. At the current price the shares are on 4.2x our FY2026 earnings, 0.6x book value and a 8.3% dividend yield [S0].

The company is a downstream palm refiner, not a plantation. It buys crude palm oil, palm kernel and wheat and sells cooking oil, margarine, shortening, specialty fats and traded flour, almost all of it into the Indonesian domestic market [S4]. Purchases of commodities were the overwhelming majority of cost of goods sold in FY2025 [F6]. The consequence is that the palm price moves revenue up and down without moving profit nearly as much: what the company earns is the spread between feedstock and refined product.

Our variant view is that the market is pricing this spread as if it were permanently broken. The shares change hands below book value and at a low multiple of the earnings the business has just demonstrated, in a year when nine-month net profit rose more than half [F19]. Book value per share is 3,382.6 against a price of Rp2,150 [S0], and equity has grown further since the last balance-sheet date [S0]. A company earning a mid-teens return on equity and paying out about a third of it is not obviously worth a discount to book; the reason it trades there is that 13.9% of the shares are in public hands and the daily traded value is IDR66.7m [S0]. We apply the house liquidity discount of 30.0% to our fundamental value and still reach a target well above the price, which is why the rating is BUY rather than HOLD.

Three things move the value. First, the gross spread: our base case carries a gross margin of 5.8% at FY2025 input costs, which the deck's higher feedstock prices trim to 5.3% in FY2026E and 4.9% in FY2027E as the unpassed share of the cost move is absorbed [S4, S2]. Second, cash conversion: in two of the last three years net profit outran operating cash flow, and the working-capital requirement is the single biggest drag on free cash flow [S0]. Third, the register: 87.0% of the shares are owned by the Wilmar holding vehicle, and until the float widens the discount is likely to persist [S4].

The Indonesian palm complex is divided between upstream planters, who own estates and mills, and downstream refiners, who buy crude palm oil and palm kernel and convert them into edible oil, fats and oleochemicals. The downstream business is a processing-margin business: capital intensity is low relative to revenue, working capital is large relative to profit, and competitive advantage comes from feedstock access, logistics and brand distribution rather than from resource ownership. Domestic cooking-oil policy has been a recurring intervention point, with price ceilings and export levies changing the split of value between growers, refiners and consumers.

PT Wilmar Cahaya Indonesia is an integrated vegetable-oil processor headquartered in Jakarta with its factory in the Jababeka industrial estate at Cikarang, Bekasi, and a second site at Pontianak in West Kalimantan [S4]. It was listed in 1996 as PT Cahaya Kalbar and renamed in 2013 after the Wilmar group took control; it is an indirect subsidiary of Wilmar International Limited, the Singapore-listed agribusiness group [S5]. It has no operating subsidiaries and no minority interests [S4].

The business model is refining and trading, not growing. The company purchases crude palm oil, palm kernel and wheat, and sells refined and fractionated products. In FY2025 purchases of commodities were 9,136 IDR bn against cost of goods sold of 9,285.9 [S4, F6]. That single ratio explains the financial shape of the company: revenue of 9,733.3 produced gross profit of 447.4, an operating margin in the low single digits, and a business whose profitability is decided by the width of the processing spread and by how well it manages the working capital that a commodity book requires [S4].

The product mix has three meaningful lines. CPO and its derivatives are the largest, at 4,670 IDR bn of FY2025 sales; palm kernel products were 3,390 IDR bn, growing far faster than everything else, at 70.7%; and traded wheat flour was 1,050 IDR bn [S4]. The nine-month 2026 figures show the same ordering but a different dynamic: CPO and derivatives at 3,820 IDR bn, palm kernel at 3,170 IDR bn and flour at 1,020 IDR bn, with the kernel line again the fastest grower [S2]. Beyond these, the company sells specialty fats for confectionery and bakery use — cocoa butter substitutes and replacers, filling and coating fats, ice-cream and milk-fat replacers, margarine and shortening — and processes illipe seed into illipe fat for export [S4]. The branded portfolio it distributes includes group brands in cooking oil and flour as well as its own packing formats [S4].

Geographically the company has become a domestic business. Domestic sales were 9,520 IDR bn of FY2025 revenue, with exports of only 211 IDR bn and no CPO export contribution in either FY2025 or FY2024 [S4]. Nine-month 2026 domestic sales were 8,110 IDR bn [S2]. This is a deliberate re-pointing of the book toward the domestic market, and it matters for how the company is exposed to policy: export duty and levy changes, which dominate the economics of an exporter, are largely irrelevant to CEKA, while domestic price policy is central.

The stated strategy is volume growth, a richer product mix and cost discipline. The board describes FY2025 as a year in which it held production and sales capacity while raw-material costs and margin pressure rose, and it targets higher production volume and a stronger value-added sales mix for 2026, with a published pre-tax profit target of 268 IDR bn [S4]. Capital spending is small and directed at the Pontianak palm-kernel plant, which was in construction in progress at end-FY2025 [F12, F28]. The work packages were substantially advanced by the balance-sheet date — the press-machine installation was 98.0% complete with an April 2026 target, and electrical and building work carried targets through June 2026 — so this is a 2026 completion, not a 2027 project [F38]. Nine-month pre-tax profit of IDR322.8bn already exceeds the full-year pre-tax target on a like-for-like basis [S10, F39].

On competitive position, CEKA is a challenger, not the leader. The Indonesian downstream palm industry is dominated by the refining arms of the large groups, and CEKA's scale is small: 354.0 employees and revenue of 9,733.3 [S0, S4]. Its advantages are its parent's feedstock and trading network, its long-standing domestic customer relationships and its food-safety certifications rather than any ownership of raw material [S4, S7].

Indonesia is the world's largest palm producer and the downstream refining industry is large, domestic-demand-led and structurally long. The industry association's data show domestic consumption still growing: cumulative January-August 2026 domestic consumption of palm products was 17,523 '000 t, and August biodiesel uptake alone reached 1,350 '000 t [S8]. Export volumes recovered in August as well [S8]. The domestic market is the growth engine, which is exactly the market CEKA serves.

The palm price is the industry's headline variable and our agricultural deck is the anchor for it. The deck has CPO at US$1,007/t a tonne for FY2025, US$1,135/t for FY2026 and a 2027 marker of US$1,240/t, easing back to US$1,210/t and US$1,180/t before a long-run anchor of US$1,150/t [deck: d.agri.cpo]. The deck's logic is a weather-driven 2027 premium followed by normalisation. For a refiner, the shape of that path matters less than the level of the spread, because a higher feedstock price with full pass-through raises revenue and leaves gross profit roughly unchanged in absolute terms [S4].

The deck prices export CPO, and the domestic market CEKA trades in settles at a different level. In the window that set the November 2026 reference price the Indonesian CPO exchange averaged US$869/t a tonne, the Malaysian exchange US$1,089/t and Rotterdam higher still [S9]. The deck's FY2026 marker sits close to the Malaysian print and above the Indonesian one; the gap is the export duty and levy wedge, not a different view of the market. Because CEKA buys and sells domestically, we use the deck only for the direction and shape of the feedstock move, and we flag it for review against the November domestic print rather than treating the export level as CEKA's revenue price [S9, F33].

Policy is the second driver and it cuts both ways. The government sets a monthly CPO reference price that fixes export duty and levy: for November 2026 the reference price was US$979/t a tonne, with duty of US$124/t a tonne plus a levy of one eighth of the reference price [S9]. Because CEKA sells domestically, it does not pay those charges; but the duty and levy set the arbitrage between selling at home and exporting, and therefore the domestic price it can charge. Domestic cooking-oil price policy — a ceiling on subsidised packaged oil — is the constraint that can prevent a refiner passing a feedstock spike through to consumers, and it is the main way regulation reaches this company's margin [S4].

Competition in refining is intense and the product is largely undifferentiated. Crude palm oil, refined bleached deodorised oil and palm kernel oil are commodities; specialty fats and branded consumer packs are the differentiated end, and that is where the company's value-added strategy points [S4]. The five forces read as follows. Supplier power is high in form but internal: related parties supplied 50.7% of commodity purchases in FY2025 [F37], which is simultaneously an advantage, in reliable supply and trade finance, and a governance exposure, because the purchase price is a group transfer price. Buyer power is moderate in number but concentrated in fact: two related-party customers took about 45.0% and 14.0% of nine-month 2026 revenue [F35, F36]. New entrants face certification, distribution and working-capital barriers but not capital-intensity barriers. Substitutes exist at the consumer level in the form of other cooking oils. Rivalry is high, which is why a mid-single-digit gross margin is the norm rather than an aberration [S4].

The moat, such as it is, is distribution density and group integration rather than brand. Domestic reach into the general trade and modern trade channels, and the ability to source feedstock from the parent's network, are the mechanisms; the quality screen's test is whether they are widening, and the evidence does not show that. Market share is not disclosed and the company does not publish a share estimate [S4], so we treat it as a price-taker in refined products and a share-gainer only in the kernel line, where sales grew far faster than the market [S8, F45].

External influences are the palm price and its weather driver, the rupiah, and interest rates. The macro deck has the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD to the dollar for FY2027 [deck: macro]; because CEKA buys and sells in rupiah, a weaker rupiah raises its costs and its selling prices together, with a second-order effect on the spread rather than a first-order one. The rate backdrop matters only through the discount rate, since the company has no debt [S4].

**Reading the net-debt/EBITDA row — table note.** That row is the template's mechanical cash roll-forward — forecast profit plus depreciation added to the FY2025 closing cash — and it cannot carry the one-off asset build described below, so it is not the balance sheet the valuation uses; the forecast years of the row should be disregarded. The row is generated by the engine from the model's own cash line and cannot be suppressed from the analyst files, so it is footnoted here instead. The valuation and the rest of this section take net cash from the 30 September 2026 statement of financial position, where the company still held net cash but only a fraction of the FY2025 close after the third-quarter outflow [S0]. Read the row as an operating-cash view, not as a forecast of reported net debt.

Revenue has grown in every year of the last five, from 6,143.8 in FY2022 to 9,733.3 in FY2025, and on to a nine-month 2026 figure of 8,340 IDR bn [S4, S2]. Almost all of that growth is price and mix rather than volume: the palm price rose and the kernel line grew faster than the rest of the book [F7, F8]. Profit did not follow the same path. Net profit was 220.7, 153.6, 324.9 and 194.6 across the four years, and gross margin moved in a band between the mid-fives and the high-sixes before falling to 4.6% in FY2025, when cost of goods sold grew faster than revenue [S4]. This is the signature of a spread business: revenue is a commodity price, profit is a margin.

Our forecast restores the margin rather than extending the trough. We carry 5.8% at FY2025 input costs, just under the four-year average and above the FY2025 trough; the engine then applies the 96.0% pass-through, so the realised margin is 5.3% in FY2026E and 4.9% in FY2027E as the deck's CPO and wheat markers land, between the nine-month actual and the FY2025 trough [S2, S4]. That is the model's whole margin story: no expansion, and no trough extension. Revenue grows by 17.5% in FY2026 on the nine-month run-rate, then by 9.0% as the deck's 2027 palm marker lands, and by low single digits thereafter as the deck glides the palm price back toward its long-run anchor [S2, S4]. That produces revenue of 11,436.6 in FY2026 and 12,465.9 in FY2027, EBIT of 375.6 and 366.3, and net profit of 303.2 and 300.0. Earnings per share are 509.5 and 504.3 [model].

The restraint in the out-years is deliberate and is the one place we model a fade. Because only part of a feedstock move is passed through, a rising palm price compresses the percentage margin even as it lifts revenue, and EBIT grows only with the rupiah cost base, from 366.3 to 432.4 over three years. That is not a cautious assumption imposed on a good business; it is what the history shows, where revenue grew by more than half over four years and EBIT went from 274.5 to 250.1 [S4].

Costs are simple. Operating expenses run at about 2.0% of revenue, mostly selling, distribution and administration, and they scale with volume [S4]. Two lines are restated from the audited accounts, and both matter because the data pack had history on a different basis from the forecast. The first is operating profit. The pack's FY2025 EBIT includes other income; the LK's own operating profit is IDR250.1bn, and in FY2024 the pack went the other way and treated other income as part of the operating result, where the LK reports IDR391.0bn [S4, F46, F47]. We restate both years to the LK's operating line, so history is gross profit less operating expenses, exactly how the forecast is built, and other income stays where the LK puts it, below the operating line. The second is depreciation: the pack carries only the cash-flow line, while the audited accounts show total depreciation charged to operations of IDR26.1bn in FY2025 and IDR26.9bn in FY2024, split between cost of goods sold, selling, general and administrative and other operating expense [F4, F5]. We restate to the total, which is what the audited accounts charge. Together the corrections put FY2025 EBITDA at 276.1 and FY2024 at IDR417.8bn, on the forecast's basis; net profit and the reported cash flows are unchanged, and the depreciation add-back is what funds free cash flow in a business with almost no capital spending.

Cash flow is where the story is least comfortable. EBITDA of 276.1 produced modelled free cash flow of -137.4 in FY2025, because working capital absorbed 324.7 [S0]. Operating cash flow was negative in the twelve months to September 2026 as well [S0]. The company funds a large receivables and inventory book out of a modest equity base, and when revenue grows quickly the asset build consumes the profit. The nine-month outflow is not a working-capital release: on the pack's quarterly balance sheet both trade receivables and inventory rose between December and September, and trade payables rose by more, so trade working capital was roughly flat. The cash went three ways instead — the June dividend, the gross trade-asset build that supplier credit financed rather than equity, and a large move in non-current assets [S0, S6].

That non-current move is the one item in this report we cannot identify, and it deserves to be stated plainly. Non-current assets were IDR279.0bn at end-FY2025, mostly net fixed assets with deferred tax assets, a non-current tax-refund claim and a small residual making up the rest [S4, F48, F50]. At 30 September 2026 the non-current block was far larger while net fixed assets had fallen, so the increase is not plant: it is a long-term item that the annual report does not contain and that we do not have, because the company publishes annual reports on its website and the interim statement itself is not in our archive [S0, S4]. The entire move happened in the September quarter, not gradually: on the pack's quarterly balance sheet the non-current block is essentially unchanged at mid-year and jumps only at 30 September, in the same quarter that cash fell by roughly the same amount while receivables and payables both rose, so it is a single third-quarter transaction rather than a slow asset build [S0]. That timing matters for the tripwire: a one-quarter placement is more consistent with a group treasury or related-party transaction than with a tax claim that accrues through the year. We therefore do not name it. The candidates are a non-current tax-recovery claim, an advance for asset purchases, or a long-term related-party receivable. The first is the one most consistent with the operating cash flow, because tax and levy prepayments leave through operating cash while an asset purchase would not; the other two would be far more serious, and if the item turns out to be a receivable from the group it is the governance tripwire discussed in the governance section. We put it in the valuation bridge in neither direction: if it is a tax claim the DCF is missing an asset, and if it is a related-party receivable the loss is not yet in our numbers. That unresolved item, not the spread, is the largest single analytical gap in this initiation.

The model's year-end cash line is mechanical and should be read as such. It rolls forward from the FY2025 close and cannot carry an asset build the template does not represent, so its FY2026E net cash is not a forecast of what will be on the balance sheet: the actual cash at the September date was a fraction of the FY2025 close [S0]. For the same reason we do not source a fourth-quarter cash swing from the annual free-cash-flow figure; the year is the nine months we can see plus an assumed fourth quarter the filings do not yet show. Our model carries working capital at 14.0% of revenue, so working capital absorbs IDR128.2bn in FY2026 against net profit of IDR303.2bn, and free cash flow to the firm after that build is IDR163.4bn — the two numbers are separate, and it is the first, not the second, that is the working-capital drag. The build normalises from FY2028 as revenue growth slows [S0]. The valuation does not use the projected cash line at all: it takes net debt from the 30 September 2026 statement of financial position [S0].

The balance sheet is unlevered. There are no borrowings and no lease liability anywhere in the FY2025 statement of financial position; the only financial liability of any size is the long-term employee-benefit obligation, and the entire financing cash outflow in FY2025 was the dividend [S4]. Interest expense was 0.1 IDR m, not the figure the data pack shows: the pack's line is the tax-penalty interest the accounts book inside other operating expense, so pre-tax profit is unaffected [F40] [S4]. Equity was 2,012.7 at end-FY2025 and 2,226.6 in our FY2026 estimate, and net debt was -303.6, a net cash position, before the 2026 asset build [S4, S0]. A company with no debt and a large domestic receivables book is not at liquidity risk, but it is dependent on the group for trade terms.

Capital allocation is dividend-led. The dividend declared for FY2025 was Rp150/share per share, paid in June 2026 [S6]. Payout has ranged from just over a quarter to just under half of profit over four years as the board has held a rupiah dividend rather than a ratio; we model 35.0%, which implies a modest step-up in the rupiah dividend on recovering earnings [S6, S4]. Capital expenditure was 21.3 IDR bn in FY2025, roughly equal to depreciation, so the asset base is being maintained rather than expanded, and the only growth project is the Pontianak kernel plant [F12, F28].

The earnings-quality screen, run in full, gives a mixed but not disqualifying result. On accruals the card's output is the three-year ratio of net profit less operating cash flow to average total assets, and it prints at or above the ten per cent threshold the card treats as earnings outrunning cash in two of the three years: eleven per cent in FY2025, sixteen per cent in FY2024 and a negative twenty-one per cent in FY2023 [S0]. The FY2025 print is auditable line by line: net profit of IDR194.6bn against operating cash flow of IDR-78.0bn, on year-end total assets of IDR2,486.5bn — the ratio uses the average of the two year-ends, which is close enough to the closing figure not to change the print [S4, S0]. FY2024 was the wider of the two, with net profit of IDR324.9bn against operating cash flow of IDR-18.1bn [S4]. The gap is an asset build rather than an accounting choice, with prepaid taxes the largest single swing item in those years [S0, S4]. Two prints at or above the threshold are optics-class, not manipulation-class: the cash is either owed back to the company or tied up in a growing commodity book, it reverses when growth slows, and the FY2023 ratio is negative — cash earnings ahead of accounting earnings — which is the opposite of the pattern a fabricated-revenue case leaves. It has not reversed yet, and the twelve months to September 2026 were negative again [S0], which is why the working-capital intensity is carried in the forecast rather than assumed away. On divergence, receivables fell year on year in FY2025 even as revenue rose by more than a fifth, which is the opposite of the classic red flag [S4]. Inventory grew more slowly than cost of goods sold [S4]. On the IDX regime, the company is not on the special monitoring board and carries no special notation, but its public register is very small: 13.9% on the exchange's free-float measure against 87.0% held by the controlling vehicle [S0, S4]. On related parties, the flows are the screen's central fact, and they run both ways: two related-party customers accounted for about 45.0% and 14.0% of nine-month 2026 revenue (3,720 IDR bn and 1,210 IDR bn), and related parties supplied 50.7% of FY2025 commodity purchases [F35, F36, F37]. The balances are 397 IDR bn receivable and 300 IDR bn payable to affiliates, roughly two fifths of the receivables book and five sixths of the payables book [S4]. That is the modal value-destruction channel in Indonesia; it is disclosed, priced on arm's-length terms according to the board, and unverified by us. On structure, there are no pledges disclosed, no rights issue, no revaluation reserve and no auditor change; the auditor is an Ernst & Young member firm with an unmodified opinion for FY2025 [S4].

A discounted cash flow is the right primary method for this company, and the cross-checks are weak by construction. CEKA is a spread business with essentially no debt, capital spending that barely exceeds depreciation, and a working-capital requirement that is a stable share of revenue; those are the conditions in which a free-cash-flow model is informative. The alternatives are worse: a P/E on trailing earnings is struck on a margin trough, and an EV/EBITDA multiple on a business with a mid-single-digit gross margin and no capital intensity tells you almost nothing about value, because EBITDA is close to EBIT and both are small relative to the revenue base [S4].

The cost of capital build is shown below. We start from a risk-free rate of 7.4% and deduct the Indonesian default spread of 1.6%, which is the sovereign credit component already inside the local risk-free rate; we then add a levered beta of 0.70 times the sum of a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, plus a company-specific governance premium of 0.5%. That gives a cost of equity of 11.0% and, with no debt, the weighted average cost of capital is 11.0% [deck: macro] [operating configuration]. The risk-free rate, the equity risk premium and the country premium are the house macro deck's rupiah inputs, and the debt weight is nil because the company has no borrowings. The beta is the FOOD_BEVERAGE industry default from the coverage config, since there is no usable regression for a name with this free float [operating configuration] [S4]. The governance premium prices the register and the terms of trade, not tradability: one Wilmar vehicle holds 87.0% of the shares against a public float of 13.9%, related parties supplied 50.7% of FY2025 commodity purchases, and two related parties took about 3,720 IDR bn and 1,210 IDR bn of nine-month 2026 sales, so a minority holder has no proxy route to value and the controlling group sets the transfer terms [S4, S0]. Half a point is the charge the house applies to comparable closed registers; it is calibrated to that disclosure rather than to a target, and the rate is re-run with it. Tradability is charged separately and once, as the 30.0% discount below, so the two effects are not double-counted. The resulting cost of equity and WACC of 11.0% sit inside the house compounder card's IDR band of eleven to thirteen per cent — the premium is what lifts the raw build into that band — and that is the rate applied in the model, with the bear scenario testing a half-point higher rate and the bull a half-point lower [S4, S0].

The DCF is below. It runs ten explicit years, which is long enough to fade the 2027 palm premium out of the margin and short enough not to pretend we know the 2035 spread. Terminal value contributes 50.2% of the value, on a terminal growth rate of 4.0% — below the macro deck's long-run nominal GDP for Indonesia, and consistent with a rupiah-denominated price that grows with the cost base rather than with real volume [deck: macro]. On that basis the enterprise value is IDR2,832.4bn and the DCF value per share is Rp4,808 [model].

**The multiple-survival test.** The compounder card asks what exit multiple the target implies and whether the DCF is a fade or a re-rating in disguise, and the honest answer is that it is a re-rating. Terminal value carries 50.2% of the enterprise value of IDR2,832.4bn; struck on FY2035E EBITDA of IDR481.1bn, it implies an exit EV/EBITDA of a little under eight times. The entry is 3.5x last year's EBITDA, and a little over three times our FY2026E on the September net cash the valuation uses — the 2.2x the engine prints for FY2026E sits on its mechanical cash roll-forward, the line the table note above says to disregard, and it understates the entry. An exit a little under eight times against an entry a little over three is roughly two and a half times the entry multiple, so this is not a fade with a free terminal value: it is the cash flow valued at a normal multiple, and the gap between three times and seven times is the thesis. What the DCF does not assume is that the multiple keeps rising after the first forecast year — its own enterprise value is about seven times FY2026E EBITDA and the terminal multiple is only a little above that — so the expansion sits between the price and the valuation, not inside the forecast [model].

**The reinvestment test.** Growth in the terminal year is manufactured, not declared. Terminal growth of 4.0% is the reinvestment rate times the return on incremental capital, and the forecast pins both: in FY2035E, capex of IDR41.8bn less depreciation of IDR45.2bn, plus a working-capital build of IDR90.1bn, puts back about a quarter of after-tax operating profit, and a quarter of NOPAT funding four per cent of growth implies a return on incremental capital of roughly fifteen per cent, three or four points above the 11.0% cost of capital. That return is defensible on this asset base rather than asserted: after-tax EBIT over net working capital plus net fixed assets was in the low twenties in FY2024 and about the cost of capital in the FY2025 trough [S4], so the terminal figure sits inside the two years we can measure. In the build years the reinvestment rate is higher, four to five tenths of after-tax operating profit, because growth here is funded by receivables and inventory rather than by plant [model]. The terminal reinvestment rate is the assumption a sceptic should push first: lifting it to the level at which the mature business earns no excess return takes about a twentieth off the DCF value.

**Held at the entry multiple.** Run the same DCF with the exit struck at the entry multiple instead of the Gordon multiple and it loses about three tenths of its value; carried through the same weights, the probability-weighted target falls to within a tenth of the Rp2,150 price and the expected total return falls to roughly the cost of equity. That is the sensitivity the card asks for, and it is the way to read the call: if the register never re-rates, a holder earns the 8.3% dividend and the forward roll and nothing more, which is what a fairly valued stock pays. The BUY is a claim that part of the gap closes within twelve months, not that the shares reach the DCF's multiple in one year — the target is struck 30.0% below the probability-weighted fundamental value, so a permanent part of the discount is conceded up front, and the 48.8% expected return is the payment for taking the convergence bet. The signposts at the end of this section are what would show the bet is being lost [model].

The two market cross-checks sit well below the DCF, and the gap is explainable rather than alarming. The P/E method applies a multiple of 8.0 — the average of the peer median and CEKA's own four-year history, which has four observations from FY2022 to FY2025, not five — to last year's trough earnings, which gives Rp2,613. The EV/EBITDA method applies 5.4 to FY2025 EBITDA and gives Rp2,569. Both are -45.7% and -46.6% below the DCF [model]. The reason is the denominator: FY2025 was the year the margin collapsed, with net profit of 194.6 against 324.9 the year before [S4]. On our FY2026 estimate the same blended P/E would produce a value close to the DCF, which tells us the multiple itself is not out of line with the cash-flow view; it is the earnings base that is stale. The blended multiple being above CEKA's own mean is the arithmetic of applying a peer-blended multiple to trough earnings: on the four-year average earnings the same blend is in line with the stock's own history. We weight the methods 60.0%, 30.0% and 10.0% as the industry template requires and show them side by side.

**The float discount is charged twice on part of the blend, and we keep it that way.** Forty per cent of the blend is a multiple, and each multiple is the average of a peer median and CEKA's own four-year history. The own-history leg is struck at prices this register has already set, so on that slice the 30.0% discount is charged twice — an overlap worth about a twelfth of the target. We disclose it rather than remove it. The own-history multiple is the only direct evidence of what this register pays for CEKA's earnings, and pricing the whole blend on peer-only multiples would import a premium from larger, more liquid food companies whose register this float cannot reach; the blends the engine prints, 8.0 times earnings and 5.4 times EBITDA, are that average, not the peer leg alone. Removing the overlap would lift the target by roughly a twelfth and would not change the rating, so keeping it is the conservative of the two defensible choices — a disclosed conservatism, not an unexplained haircut [model].

Sensitivity is to the spread, not to the discount rate. A one-percentage-point change in gross margin is worth about a third of the Rp4,808 DCF value per share, and close to twice the swing from a one-point change in the cost of capital — the arithmetic signature of a business with a thin margin on a large revenue base. Read off the centre row of the second grid, the move from one point of margin below our base to one point above is the widest single-driver range in the report, and it survives the liquidity discount: the same point is worth close to two fifths of the target a holder actually receives. The table below shows the range [model].

What the price implies is the cleanest way to state the variant view. At Rp2,150 the company is valued at IDR1,279.2bn, which on our FY2026 estimates is 4.2x earnings and 0.6x book, with a 13.9% free-cash-flow-to-equity yield; on the 31 December 2025 balance sheet, with the net cash the company still held at that date, it is 3.5x EBITDA [S0, model]. We quote the year-end multiple because that is the balance sheet the engine's multiple line computes it on; struck on the September net cash the same earnings give a higher multiple, because the group spent most of that cash in the nine months, and it is the September net cash that the valuation uses. For a company that earns a mid-teens return on equity, sustains a book value per share of 3,382.6 and pays out about a third of its profit, a multiple below book implies the market expects returns to fall toward the cost of capital permanently, or applies a discount for the register. Our base case assumes the return on equity holds near 14.3% and applies a 30.0% discount for the float on top; the residual gap is the opportunity [S0].
The downside risks, with our read of likelihood and impact:

**Domestic price policy (high likelihood, high impact).** A tightening of the cooking-oil price ceiling, or a change in the levy structure that raises the domestic feedstock price relative to the retail price, would compress the spread directly. This is the single most important regulatory risk and it has precedent in the policy's frequent revision [S4, S9].

**A feedstock spike without pass-through (medium likelihood, high impact).** The deck has CPO rising to US$1,240/t in FY2027 on an El Nino-driven crop shortfall [deck: d.agri.cpo]. If the domestic retail price cannot follow, the margin takes the hit rather than the consumer. Our base case passes most of the move through; the bear case does not [S4].

**Group transfer pricing (medium likelihood, high impact if it materialises).** This is the risk that explains why a profitable, unlevered company trades below book, and it is quantified in the flows rather than the balances. Related parties supplied 50.7% of FY2025 commodity purchases, and two related-party customers took about 45.0% and 14.0% of nine-month 2026 revenue [F35, F36, F37]. A change in transfer terms would move profit without any change in volume, and minority holders have no mechanism to prevent it. The bear case contains such a reset, and its size is the one assumption in the scenario set that needs an argument: a little over one per cent on the affiliate purchase price, where about half the purchase book sits [F37], moves the gross margin six tenths of a point — about a quarter of the two-point margin swing the accounts already show between FY2024 and FY2025. It is a fraction of a move the company has delivered, not a catastrophe [S4, F1, F3].

**Cash conversion and working capital (high likelihood, medium impact).** In two of the last three years operating cash flow was below net profit, and the twelve months to September 2026 were negative [S0]. If the asset build that produced the negative operating cash flow is structural rather than a timing difference, the free cash flow that supports the dividend and the valuation is smaller than the DCF assumes. The unidentified non-current item is the sharpest form of that risk: the cash has already left, and whether it comes back as a tax refund, a purchase asset or a group receivable changes the equity value without touching the earnings forecast [S0, S4].

**Liquidity and float (high likelihood, medium impact).** The free float is 13.9% and the daily traded value is IDR66.7m [S0]. A holder cannot build or exit a position without moving the price, which is precisely what the 30.0% discount in our target reflects.

**Governance and control (structural, medium impact).** The controlling shareholder owns 87.0% of the shares [S4]. Minority influence is limited to voting on routine resolutions; there is no independent path to a control premium unless the parent chooses to sell. The one upside branch the register offers is a tender: a parent bid at book value would give minorities 3,382.6 per share, above the current price, and it is the only event that closes the discount without waiting for the market [S4, F25].

**Currency and rates (low likelihood, low impact).** The company has no debt and matches rupiah costs to rupiah revenue; the rupiah matters through the dollar-denominated palm price and the cost of imported wheat [S0].
**Execution on the kernel plant (medium likelihood, low impact).** The Pontianak project is small relative to the revenue base, so delay affects growth rather than solvency [F28].

The scenarios mirror each other on the two operating drivers, revenue growth and gross margin, and on cost of capital; the bear shocks the WACC up by a half point while the bull shocks it down a half point, a symmetrical rate attack. The base case is weighted at one half and bear and bull at a quarter each. The bear case combines the operating squeeze — a domestic ceiling that blocks pass-through on a feedstock spike — with the one-sided group-pricing risk: a transfer-pricing reset in a book where related parties are half the purchase cost and most of the customer base. The bull case is the mirror-image operating recovery, and it is not generic: the Pontianak kernel plant completes on its 2026 schedule, the kernel line that grew 70.7% in FY2025 keeps taking mix, and the FY2026 guidance beat already in our base carries into FY2027 [F38, F45, F19, F39].

The three values the table prints — Rp4,180, Rp2,127 and Rp6,777 — are all pre-liquidity-discount, and the price they are being read against is not: the 30.0% discount is applied to the probability-weighted value when the target is struck. On a like-for-like basis a holder's three branches are seven tenths of the tabulated figures: about Rp4,180 less its discount for the base, a little under three thousand; about Rp6,777 less its discount for the bull, a little under five thousand; and about Rp2,127 less its discount for the bear, a little under fifteen hundred, which lands roughly a third below the Rp2,150 price rather than at it. That is the correction that matters to the call: the bear is a real loss of about a third, not a flat-to-price value trap, and no part of the downside protection in this report comes from comparing a gross scenario value with a net price.

Read that way the risk-reward is upward-skewed on probabilities but not floored: after the same discount the bear costs about a third of the price, the base returns a little over a third, and the bull a little more than doubles it. Weighted at one half, a quarter and a quarter, the value after the discount is Rp3,021 — the 48.8% total return we lead with, against a pre-discount probability-weighted value of Rp4,316. The skew is in the bull's multiple, not in a floor under the bear: a holder who gets the bear loses about a third of the price, and the reason to own the shares is the distribution's centre, not its left tail.

The signposts that would change our view, in order of importance: a fall in gross margin below the FY2025 trough for two consecutive quarters, which would say the spread is structurally broken rather than cyclical; a material rise in related-party receivables relative to revenue, which would say the group is using the listed entity as a funding vehicle; a change in the disclosed related-party purchase share, which is the transfer-pricing tripwire; and a free-float widening or a tender that changes the register, which would justify removing part of the liquidity discount.

Ownership is concentrated and the group is the ultimate parent. PT Sentratama Niaga Indonesia holds 87.0% and the public holds the rest in blocks each below five per cent [S4]. Sentratama sits inside the Wilmar International group, and the company describes itself as an indirect subsidiary of Wilmar International Limited [S5]. The exchange's free-float measure is 13.9% and the annual report's controlling stake is 87.0%; the two are measured on different dates and treat the residual blocks differently, but they say the same thing, that the public register is very small [S0, S4]. We are not aware of any pledge of the controlling stake, any special monitoring-board status, or any administrative sanction; the annual report discloses no legal proceedings of consequence [S4, S0].

The board is led by Erry Tjuatja as President Director, and the annual report carries the standard statement of directors' and commissioners' responsibility for the accounts [S4]. The auditor is Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, a member firm of Ernst & Young, which issued an unmodified opinion on the FY2025 financial statements dated 17 March 2026 [S4]. There has been no auditor down-tier change and no restatement.

Related-party dealings are the main governance fact and they are disclosed rather than hidden. Related parties supplied 50.7% of commodity purchases in FY2025, and two related-party customers took about 45.0% and 14.0% of nine-month 2026 revenue [F35, F36, F37]. At end-FY2025 the trade payable to related parties was 300 IDR bn and the trade receivable was 397 IDR bn [S4]. The board states that transactions are on arm's-length terms and that the necessary procedures were followed [S4]. We cannot verify the pricing and treat it as an ongoing exposure rather than a finding; it is the reason the bear case now includes a transfer-pricing shock rather than an operating shock alone. There have been no discounted private placements, no rights issues and no share-count change since listing [S4].

One balance-sheet fact sits outside that disclosed picture, and we flag it rather than price it. Between the FY2025 accounts and the September interim, non-current assets grew by an amount that plant cannot explain, because net fixed assets fell over the same period, and the annual report contains no such line [S4, F48]. If that item is a receivable from the Wilmar group or an advance to an affiliate, it is the same value-destruction channel the related-party flows above describe, executed on the asset side of the balance sheet instead of through the trading account; if it is a tax-recovery claim it is benign and recoverable. We cannot tell which from the archived record, so we assume neither and neither deduct nor add it in the valuation. It is the first item we will reconcile when the interim accounts reach us, and the answer will settle whether the governance risk in this name is a pricing question or a balance-sheet one.

The dividend record is good for a small cap: a dividend has been declared and paid in each of the last five years, held flat for a period and then raised, with the FY2025 dividend of Rp150/share paid in June 2026 [S6, S4]. The payout has been a rupiah amount rather than a fixed ratio, which is a deliberate policy choice and one reason we model a ratio rather than extrapolate the amount.

On ESG, the sustainability report we archived describes food-safety and quality certification — the FSSC food-safety scheme, the national SNI standard, Halal certification from the Indonesian Ulema Council and BPOM-certified good manufacturing practice — rather than any sustainability certification of the palm supply chain [S7]. That is a gap worth noting: a downstream palm processor selling into domestic food manufacturing is exposed to buyer sustainability requirements and to the reputational risk of the upstream supply chain, and the company does not claim RSPO or equivalent chain-of-custody certification in the report [S7]. Its direct environmental footprint is limited, since it does not operate estates or mills, but the working-capital-intensive trading model means it is buying from many upstream sources whose practices it does not control [S4].

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 results in the first quarter of 2027, the annual general meeting and dividend approval in June, the ramp of the Pontianak kernel plant through the second half of 2026, and the monthly CPO reference price and quarterly duty resets that set the domestic price environment [S4, S9].

Between updates we monitor four things. The quarterly gross margin, which is the spread, and the palm kernel share of revenue, which is the mix [S2, S4]. The working-capital line, the prepaid-tax balance and the non-current asset lines, which decide whether the dividend is funded by cash or by the balance sheet, and which is where the unidentified long-term item will either explain itself or not [S0, S4]. The related-party purchase share and the related-party receivable balance as a share of revenue, which are the governance tripwires [S4, F37]. And the free float, since a widening of the register is the one event that would let the price converge on value without waiting for the parent to act [S0].

We also watch the palm price against the deck, and the domestic reference against the export benchmark. A move materially above the 2027 marker without a matching move in refined-product prices would be the early warning that the spread is being squeezed rather than passed through, and it would take us to the bear case before the reported margin does [S0, S9].

bear.narrative: A value-trap bear, not only an operating one. El Nino cuts the 2027 kernel and CPO crop and the domestic cooking-oil price ceiling stops the refiner passing the feedstock through, which takes 1.2 points off the spread on four points less revenue growth. On top of that the group resets its transfer terms: related parties are 50.67% of commodity purchases [F37] and about 59% of sales [F35, F36], so a little over one per cent on the affiliate purchase price - about a quarter of the 2.2-point gross-margin swing the accounts already show between FY2024 and FY2025 [F3, F2] - takes a further 0.6 points, with no volume change and no mechanism for minorities to prevent it. The 13.9% register and the negative operating cash flow keep the illiquidity discount in place throughout, so the shares do not re-rate even on trough earnings; a half-point higher cost of capital, the mirror of the bull case's half-point lower, takes a further slice of the same value without touching the operating story.

bull.narrative: The Pontianak palm-kernel plant completes on its 2026 schedule - the press installation was 98% and electrical work 86% at end-2025, with April-June 2026 targets [F38] - and ramps into a kernel line that grew 70.7% in FY2025 and 35% in nine-month 2026 [F8, F21]. Kernel and specialty-fat mix take gross margin back toward the FY2024 6.8% level (+1.2 points) on four points more revenue growth, and the FY2026 guidance beat already in our base (nine-month pre-tax profit of Rp322.80bn against the Rp268.16bn full-year pre-tax target [F55, F39]) carries into 2027. A half-point lower cost of capital, mirroring the bear's half-point higher, is applied on the same operating numbers.

12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +17.5%: nine-month 2026 revenue was Rp8.34trn, +19.13% [F18], and the deck has CPO at USD1,135/t for FY2026 versus USD1,007/t realised in FY2025 (fund record reviewed 2026-10-27), so the fourth quarter should hold the pace at a slightly slower rate. FY2027E +9.0% carries the deck's FY2027 CPO marker of USD1,240 (+9.2% on 2026) with flat-to-modest volume. FY2028E and FY2029E +3.0%: the deck glides CPO back to USD1,210 and then USD1,180, so revenue growth collapses to volume plus rupiah translation once the weather premium clears. FY2030E and the long run +4.0%: the deck's long-run CPO anchor of USD1,150 escalates with the IDR cost base (lt_escalation: idr), which is about 4% nominal once 2% volume is added. This is a spread business, not a compounder: FY2022-FY2025 revenue grew 6.4% a year in a rising palm market and net profit fell, so growth above inflation is not assumed past the deck's 2027 marker.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 5.8% at FY2025 input costs. Realised gross margin was 6.86% (FY2022), 5.46% (FY2023), 6.82% (FY2024) and 4.60% (FY2025, when COGS grew 24.53% against 21.62% revenue [F3]), and 5.49% in nine-month 2026 [F18, S2]; the four-year average is 5.94%. The spread is set by refined-product competition and product mix (palm kernel sales grew 70.7% in FY2025 [F8]), not by the palm price itself, so the four-year average with the 2025 trough in the sample is the right anchor; 5.8% strips out the 2024 peak. No margin expansion is assumed. The engine applies the 4% unpassed share of the feedstock move to this base, so the realised path is about 5.3% in FY2026E and 4.9% in FY2027E as the deck's CPO and wheat markers land, between the 9M-2026 actual and the FY2025 trough; the report states the realised path, not the base input.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: 88%. Purchases of commodities were 98.4% of cost of goods sold in FY2025 [F6]; CPO and palm kernel products are Rp8.06trn of the Rp9.73trn revenue [F7, F8] and wheat flour Rp1.05trn [F9], so CPO and kernel feedstock is about 88% of the cost base and wheat the other 10%. The split inside "purchases of commodities" is not filed, which is why this is derived from the revenue mix rather than a single disclosed line.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: 96%. A refiner buys feedstock at market and sells refined product off the same market, so the great majority of a CPO move reaches the selling price: realised gross margin did not track the palm price across the last four years (CPO averaged USD886, 963, 1,007 and about 1,131 while gross margin went 6.9%, 5.5%, 6.8%, 4.6%, 5.5%). The 4% not passed is the residual squeeze a refiner carries when feedstock spikes between purchase and sale, and it is deliberately small because the evidence shows no systematic margin leak.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: 10%. Wheat flour is a traded line, Rp1.05trn of FY2025 revenue [F9], bought and resold rather than milled (the company owns no mill), so its cost is the wheat price and it is about a tenth of the consolidated cost base.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: 98%. Flour is distributed on thin fixed trading margins; the wheat price is passed through almost entirely, so a wheat move changes revenue but barely changes gross profit.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 2.0%. Opex was 2.03% of revenue in FY2025 (Rp197.3bn of Rp9,733.3bn, AR2025 p.14) and 1.89% in nine-month 2026 (gross profit Rp458.3bn less EBIT Rp301.0bn on Rp8,343.6bn revenue, [S0] quarterly data). Distribution and selling costs scale with volume, so a flat share is the right shape; the lower 2026 run-rate reflects operating leverage on a bigger revenue base.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 0.27%. Total depreciation charged to operations was Rp26.065bn in FY2025 and Rp26.861bn in FY2024 [F4, F5] on revenue of Rp9.7trn and Rp8.0trn, i.e. 0.268% and 0.336%: the charge is broad-based, with COGS Rp20.7bn, selling Rp2.2bn, G&A Rp2.3bn and other operating expense Rp0.9bn. The data pack carries only Rp5.4bn, which is why history is restated from the total. A flat 0.27% follows the fixed asset base, which is being maintained rather than expanded.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: 0.25%. Capital goods investment was Rp21.26bn in FY2025 [F12], Rp23.3bn in FY2024 and Rp10.6bn in FY2023, i.e. roughly equal to D&A, with the largest 2025 item the Pontianak palm-kernel plant in construction. 0.25% covers maintenance plus completion of that project and leaves no expansion capex that the filings do not show.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 14%. Operating working capital was Rp1,473.0bn at end-FY2025 (15.1% of revenue) and Rp1,390.6bn at 30 September 2026; 14% is the mid-point of the FY2025 close and the 12.6% latest ratio, not a Q4 rebuild. The 2026 cash outflow is not a trade working-capital release: trade receivables and inventory both rose between December and September and trade payables rose by more, so trade working capital was roughly flat and the pack's NWC falls only because other current assets did. The cash went to the June dividend, to the gross trade-asset build that supplier credit financed, and to a non-current asset build of about Rp512bn that the template cannot represent. The FY2026E cash line is therefore mechanical and the DCF takes net debt from the 30 September 2026 balance sheet instead. Working capital is still the largest single drain on FCFF at a 17% revenue growth rate.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 23%. Cash tax took 21.3% of pre-tax profit in FY2024, 21.6% in FY2023 and 27.0% in FY2025 (the high year follows a lower pre-tax base); the statutory rate is 22% and the three-year average of 23.3% is the right forward rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8.5%, but the line is immaterial: the company has no bank borrowings and no lease liability anywhere on the FY2025 statement of financial position [S4], and interest expense for FY2025 was Rp79,134 [F40]. The Rp8.3bn that the data pack labels interest expense is the tax-penalty interest the LK books inside other operating expense (note 28), not a financing cost. With debt at zero, the rate does not move the model; 8.5% is retained only as a placeholder for the IDR corporate rate a Wilmar-group entity would pay if it borrowed.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default 5.96% = interest income / opening cash across FY2023-FY2025; FY2025 interest income was Rp20.4bn on opening cash of Rp590.8bn. Cash has since fallen to Rp28.5bn at 30 September 2026, so the absolute contribution shrinks even though the rate is intact.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No borrowings are disclosed and no issuance is planned; the lease book is stable.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring non-operating income or expense beyond interest; FY2025 other items are immaterial.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: No subsidiaries with minority interests; the company has no consolidated minority balance.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 35%. The board sets a rupiah dividend, not a ratio: Rp100 in FY2022 and FY2023, Rp150 in FY2024 and FY2025 [F17], which is 27%, 39%, 27% and 46% of the respective profits. The median is 33% and the mean 35%, so 35% is the central case rather than the 46% of the depressed FY2025 base: it implies about Rp180 per share on our FY2026 estimate, a modest step up from Rp150, and an 8.4% yield at the current price.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No buyback, no rights issue, 595,000,000 shares outstanding since the 1996 IPO.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0%. Revenue is a refined-oil price times volume; the agri deck's long-run CPO anchor of USD1,150/t escalates with the Indonesian cost base, so in rupiah the long-run growth is roughly rupiah inflation minus the deck's real CPO drift, about 3-4%. That sits below the house macro deck's 5.29% real GDP growth plus 3.28% CPI (fund record), which is the ceiling the compounder card sets for terminal growth.

The report calls Rp20.7bn 'the real depreciation charge'; forward da_pct 0.21% gives Rp24.0bn. Understates the add-back the report says funds FCFF by ~Rp3-5bn a year.

S4 p.143 shows Rp43,434,888,614 is long-term employee-benefit liabilities; the income statement and cash-flow statement show interest expense of Rp79,134 (p.144 and p.146). There is no lease liability, and the interest figure is off by roughly 100x. The cited page says the opposite of the claim.
challenges.answer: The cost_of_debt basis is corrected: no borrowings and no lease liability anywhere on the balance sheet, the Rp43.4bn is long-term employee benefits, and FY2025 interest expense was Rp79,134. The pack's Rp8.3bn is tax-penalty interest booked in other operating expense (note 28), so PBT is unaffected [S4, F40].

findings.finding: fund record qc_justifications.extreme_call ends by saying the transfer-pricing tail is carried as a tripwire rather than a shock because no source sets its magnitude. That contradicts the model: scenarios.bear carries a -0.6pp transfer-pricing shock (a.gross_margin -0.018 vs bull +0.012), and the scenario.symmetry justification for the same round calls its magnitude sourced. Two BLOCK-flag justifications for the same model disagree on whether the shock exists.

The scenario.symmetry justification claims the 0.6pp is sourced in magnitude as well as direction. F37 (50.67% of purchases) and F1/F3 (2.2pp FY2024-to-FY2025 margin swing) support the direction, the 0.6pp arithmetic and the quarter-of-the-swing precedent, but no source sets the 1.2% affiliate-price reset itself.

VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY item 4 asks for the implied exit EV/EBIT, but the multiple-survival test is run on EV/EBITDA (7.7x exit vs 3.1-3.5x entry). On EBIT the exit is about 8.5x (TV 3,690.7 / FY2035 EBIT 435.9) against about 3.9x entry (EV 975.5 / FY2025 EBIT 250.1), so the conclusion holds but the card output is not stated.

Terminal ROIIC of 15.5% sits three to four points above the 11.0% WACC and is not faded to the cost of capital by year 10 (card item 3), while section 2 says the moat evidence is not widening. The report quantifies the reinvestment sensitivity (about a twentieth off the DCF) but does not name the permanent excess return as an assumption.

The bear has no branch for the unidentified Rp519bn Q3 2026 non-current item, which sections 3 and 6 call the largest analytical gap and the post-BS review leaves out of the bridge in both directions. The 25% bear therefore carries none of the balance-sheet risk the report itself describes as unresolved.

The 50bp governance premium is described as the charge the house applies to comparable closed registers, but no codified house rule for a 50bp closed-register premium was found in fund rules or operating configuration It is inside the band and lowers value (conservative), so it does not move the rating.

flags.justification: The 0.6pp transfer-pricing shock is sourced in magnitude as well as direction. Related parties supplied 50.67pc of FY2025 commodity purchases [F37], which are Rp9,136.4bn of a Rp9,285.9bn cost of goods sold [F6, F3], so a 1.2pc reset on the affiliate purchase price moves the gross margin by 0.6pp - about a quarter of the 2.2pp swing the accounts already show between the FY2024 and FY2025 margins [F1, F2, F3]. The asymmetry is deliberate and one-sided: a transfer-terms reset can only be taken from minorities, the record shows no favourable reset, and there is no mechanism by which they could demand one [S4, F37, F35, F36], while the bull's operating recovery is already carried at the mirrored +1.2pp on revenue growth and gross margin.

flags.justification: The expected return is a spread business priced at a float discount, not a stretched forecast, and what the price implies is visible in the multiples the engine prints: 4.2x our FY2026 earnings, 0.6x book and an 8.3% dividend yield on our payout, so the return needs only that the spread holds near its four-year average and that part of the register discount closes. Every input is anchored on the LK: gross margin 5.8% at FY2025 input costs is the four-year average around the FY2025 trough of 4.60% [F3], and the engine's 4% unpassed share realises 5.3% in FY2026E and 4.9% in FY2027E, not more. History is restated twice from the audited accounts — total depreciation charged to operations [F4, F5] rather than the pack's cash-flow line, and operating profit of Rp250.071bn FY2025 and Rp390.984bn FY2024 [F46, F47] rather than the pack's other-income-inclusive EBIT — so history and forecast sit on one operating basis. The company has no borrowings and interest expense of Rp79,134 [F40]. Beta is the 0.7 FOOD_BEVERAGE default, a 50bp governance premium prices the 87.02% register inside the cost of equity, and the 30% liquidity discount is applied on top for a traded value of about Rp67m a day. The three drivers are the restored spread, the kernel mix and the dividend; the bear is the mirrored operating squeeze with no re-rating, while the transfer-pricing tail is carried as a tripwire rather than a shock because no source sets its magnitude [F37, F35, F36].
